problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}$ and $C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
examples.problem: Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065461/assets/51b47f81b941fffa62d1f8402a4ef08b9b7d1636b1a37a86578311f1db192b3d.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065461/assets/a9964c0672c8859f4b4857d422e25a435ed0be907c074a22b7cc12729f051613.png) be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$
examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \},$ respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

So, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065461/assets/60eb4bbd057feab1b78fb283e951dc8c35f9a95875bd46f078c87c25b3b749c8.png)

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -5 & 7 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & 22 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}= & [\begin{aligned}\,4 & 22 \\ \,1 & 13\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
feedback.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 4-3\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
